source_text: 9.40 καὶ μὴν πρὸς τὴν ἐνανθρώπησιν αὐτοῦ ὅλον νένευκε τὸ νόημα. 9.41 ἐπειδὴ γὰρ λέγοντι αὐτῷ· «υἱὸς θεοῦ εἰμι» ἀντεφθέγγοντο· «βλασφημεῖς», ἐπεψηφίσατο αὐτῷ ὁ πατὴρ ὅτι «οὗτος μόνος ἐστὶν ὁ υἱός μου γνήσιος». 9.42 Τὸ γάρ «οὗτος» καὶ τό «ἀγαπητός» καὶ τὸ μετὰ ἄρθρου ὠνομάσθαι «υἱός» τοῦτο δηλοῖ· ἐν τούτῳ, φησίν, εὐδόκησα διὰ τῆς ἐνανθρωπήσεως αὐτοῦ τὴν σωτηρίαν ὑμῖν πορισθῆναι. 9.43 κἂν περὶ τῆς θεότητος δὲ ἐκλάβῃ τις τό «εὐδόκησα», τὸ σόφισμα αὐτῶν ἀκυροῦται· ἐπείπερ οὐ πᾶσα λέξις ῥηθεῖσα παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ μάλιστα περὶ τοῦ θεοῦ λόγου κοσμικοῦ ἔθους ἀποτελεῖ νόημα. 9.44 Ἔπειτα εἰ ἐπὶ τῷ ἤδη ὄντι υἱῷ ἔλεγεν· «ἐν ᾧ εὐδόκησα», οὐκ αἰτία ἡ εὐδοκία τῆς ὑπάρξεως αὐτοῦ εὑρίσκεται. 9.45 Ὥστε δὲ σαφέστερον τὸ ὑπὸ τῆς τοιαύτης λέξεως δηλούμενον γενέσθαι, μάρτυρι χρησώμεθα τῷ ψάλλοντι ἐν ρμθʹ ψαλμῷ· «ὅτι εὐδοκεῖ κύριος ἐν τῷ λαῷ αὐτοῦ». 9.46 οὐ γέγονεν δὲ ἡ εὐδοκία πρὸ τοῦ λαοῦ, ἀλλὰ μετ' αὐτόν. 9.47 τότε γὰρ εὐδόκει ἐν αὐτῷ καὶ εἰρήνην καὶ χάριν ἔπεμπεν, ὅτε ὀρθῶς αὐτῷ ἐλάτρευεν· ὅτε δὲ μὴ ὀρθῶς, τοὐναντίον ἢ νῦν προφητεύει· «ὅταν ἀπέκτεννεν αὐτούς, τότε ἐξεζήτουν αὐτόν»· καὶ ἐν μγʹ ψαλμῷ· «ὁ βραχίων αὐτῶν οὐκ ἔσωσεν αὐτούς, ἀλλ' ἡ δεξιά σου καὶ ὁ βραχίων σου καὶ ὁ φωτισμὸς τοῦ προσώπου σου, ὅτι εὐδόκησας ἐν αὐτοῖς», «δεξιὰν καὶ βραχίονα τοῦ θεοῦ» καί «φωτισμὸν τοῦ προσώπου αὐτοῦ» τὸν υἱὸν ἀνειπών· 9.48 καὶ ἐν ρεʹ ψαλμῷ· «μνήσθητι ἡμῶν, κύριε, ἐν τῇ εὐδοκίᾳ τοῦ λαοῦ σου». 10.ν Περὶ τοῦ λέγειν· «Εἰ ὅλος ἐστὶ γεννητικὸς ὁ ἀγέννητος θεός, οὐκ οὐσιωδῶς ἐγέννησεν» καὶ ὅτι «Εἰ μετεβλήθη ἡ οὐσία αὐτοῦ εἰς γέννημα, οὐκ ἀμετάβλητος ἡ οὐσία τοῦ θεοῦ». 10.1 Αὐτῶν καὶ τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ εἰκαῖον καὶ πλημμελὲς λέξεσιν τοιαῖσδε τεθέν· 10.2 «εἰ ὅλος ἐστὶ γεννητικὸς ὁ ἀγέννητος θεός, οὐκ οὐσιωδῶς ὁ γεννηθεὶς ἐγεννήθη, ὅλης ἐχούσης τῆς οὐσίας αὐτοῦ τὸ γεννᾶν, ἀλλ' οὐ τὸ γεννᾶσθαι.» 10.3 ἀλλ' ἀκουέτωσαν ὅτιπερ «εἰ ὅλον ἐστὶ γεννητικὸν τὸ φῶς, οὐκ οὐσιωδῶς τὸ ἀπαύγασμα γεννᾷ, ἀλλ' ἔξωθεν προσλαμβάνει, ὅλης ἐχούσης τῆς οὐσίας αὐτοῦ τὸ γεννᾶν, ἀλλ' οὐ τὸ γεννᾶσθαι». 10.4 εἰ δὲ τὸ φῶς οὐ προσλαμβάνει ἔξωθεν τὸ ἀπαύγασμα, ἀλλ' ἐκ πάσης τῆς οὐσίας αὐτὸ γεννᾷ ἀδιαστάτως, οὐδ' ὁ θεὸς ἐπεκτήσατο ἔξωθεν τὸν υἱόν, ἀλλ' ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ὑποστάσεως ἐγέννησεν ἀδιαστάτως, ἅτε ἀσώματος. ὅθεν ἀληθῶς ἐστι πατήρ. 10.5 Ἐπάγουσι πάλιν, πανταχοῦ τὴν ἐναντίαν τάξιν τῆς γραφῆς διώκοντες· «εἰ μετασχηματισθεῖσα ἡ οὐσία τοῦ θεοῦ γέννημα λέγεται, οὐκ ἀμετάβλητος ἡ οὐσία αὐτοῦ, τῆς μεταβολῆς ἐργασαμένης τὴν τοῦ υἱοῦ ἰδιοποίησιν.» 10.6 Ἀλλ' οὐδεὶς οὐδὲ τοῦτο συγχωρεῖ αὐτοῖς λέγειν. ἀλλότρια γὰρ εἶναι ταῦτα Χριστιανῶν ἡ μνημονευθεῖσα ἐλέγχει γραφή, παντὶ 6 αἱρετικῷ ἀντιβαίνουσα παγχαλέπῳ πάθει. 10.7 εἰ γὰρ μετασχηματισάμενον τὸ φῶς ἀπαύγασμα γίνεται, οὐκ ἀμετάβλητον τὸ φῶς, τῆς μεταβολῆς ἐργαζομένης τὴν τοῦ ἀπαυγάσματος ἰδιοποίησιν. 10.8 Εἰ δὲ οὐ μεταβληθὲν τὸ φῶς ἀπαύγασμα γεγέννηκεν, μεῖναν καὶ αὐτὸ φῶς καὶ ἔχον τὸ ἀπαύγασμα συμφύτως ἐξ αὐτοῦ τέλειον, καὶ ὁ θεὸς μένει ἀτρέπτως θεός, ἀπαυγάσματος ἰδίου τυγχάνων πατήρ, οὔκετι ἔξωθεν αὐτὸ προσλαβών, ἀλλ' ἐκ τῆς οὐσίας γεννήσας τέλειον. 11.ν Περὶ τῶν φλυαρούντων ὡς «ἐκ τῆς πατρὸς ὀνομασίας παρηλλαγμένη ἐστὶν ἡ οὐσία αὐτοῦ τοῦ υἱοῦ». 11.1 Αὐτὰ περὶ τῶν αὐτῶν ἀνακυκλοῦντες καὶ ἕως τοῦ παντὸς παρασημαίνοντες τῆς ἀληθείας τὸ κάλλος, ἀφιλο̣θέως καὶ τοῦτο φάσκουσιν· 11.2 ὧν τὰ ὀνόματά ἐστι διάφορα, τούτων παρηλλάχθαι καὶ τὰς οὐσίας ἀνάγκη. 11.3 φησὶν γάρ· «ἡ πατὴρ λέξις οὐ σημαίνει τὴν υἱὸς οὐδ' αὖ υἱὸς ὀνομασία δηλοῖ τὴν πατρὸς ὑπόστασινʹ. 11.4 Ἀκουέτωσαν δέ, ἓν μέν, ὅτι, εἰ μὴ καταλλήλῳ προσηγορίᾳ πεφανέρωντο αἱ θεῖαι ὑποστάσεις, ποίῳ συμβόλῳ ἄν τις χρησάμενος, μὴ λέγων τὴν πατρὸς προσηγορίαν, ἐμήνυσεν αὐτόν τε τὸν πατέρα καὶ ὅτι υἱὸν ἔχει; ἢ μὴ ὀνομάζων τὴν υἱὸς καὶ πνεῦμα προσηγορίαν, προσεφώνησεν αὐτόν τε τὸν υἱὸν ἢ τὸ πνεῦμα καὶ ὅτι ὁ μὲν υἱὸς πατέρα ἔχει, τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα τοῦ θεοῦ ἐστιν πνεῦμα; 11.5 Ἕτερον δέ, ὅτι ἐπὶ τῆς ἁγίας τριάδος–πλὴν τοῦ πατέρα λέγεσθαι τὸν ἀληθῶς ὄντα τοῦτο, καὶ τοῦ μονογενῆ καλεῖσθαι τὸν φυσικῶς γεννηθέντα, καὶ τοῦ πνεῦμα θεοῦ προσαγορεύεσθαι τὸ ἀκριβῶς τοῦτο, ὃ κέκληται, τυγχάνον τοῦ πατρός–τἄλλα πάντα ὀνόματα καθέστηκεν τὰ αὐτά, ὡς τὸ θεός, κύριος, ἅγιος, δίκαιος, ἀγαθός, φῶς, ζωή. 11.6 Οὐκοῦν τοὐναντίον, ἐπὶ τῆς μακαρίας τριάδος μόνης, ὧν τὰ ὀνόματά ἐστιν τὰ

since not every expression spoken by God, and especially about God the Word, completes a meaning of worldly custom. 9.44 Next, if he was saying of the Son who already is: 'in whom I was well pleased', the good pleasure is not found cause of his existence. 9.45 And so that what is shown by such an expression become clearer, let us use as witness the one singing in the 149th psalm: 'because the Lord is well pleased in his people'. 9.46 But the good pleasure did not come to be before the people, but after it. 9.47 For then he was well pleased in it and was sending peace and grace, when it was serving him rightly; but when not rightly, the opposite, as now he prophesies: 'when he was killing them, then they were seeking him out'; and in the 43rd psalm: 'their arm did not save them, but your right hand and your arm and the illumination of your face, because you were well pleased in them', proclaiming the Son 'right hand and arm of God' and 'illumination of his face'; 9.48 and in the 105th psalm: 'remember us, Lord, in the good pleasure of your people'. 10.ν [Chapter title:] About the saying: 'if the unbegotten God is wholly generative, he did not beget essentially', and that 'if his essence was changed into an offspring, the essence of God is not unchangeable'. 10.1 This too is theirs, the random and faulty thing, placed in words such as these: 10.2 'if the unbegotten God is wholly generative, the one begotten was not begotten essentially, his whole essence having the begetting, but not the being begotten.' 10.3 But let them hear that 'if the light is wholly generative, it does not beget the radiance essentially, but takes it on from outside, its whole essence having the begetting, but not the being begotten'. 10.4 But if the light does not take on the radiance from outside, but begets it from the whole essence without interval, neither did God acquire in addition the Son from outside, but begot from the whole hypostasis without interval, as being bodiless. Whence he truly is Father. 10.5 They bring on again, everywhere pursuing the order contrary to the Scripture: 'if the essence of God, having been transformed, is called offspring, his essence is not unchangeable, the change having worked the appropriation of the Son.' 10.6 But no one concedes them to say even this. For the Scripture mentioned refutes these things as being foreign to Christians, opposing every heretical, most grievous affliction. 10.7 For if the light, having been transformed, becomes radiance, the light is not unchangeable, the change working the appropriation of the radiance. 10.8 But if the light, not having been changed, has begotten radiance, having remained also itself light and having the radiance from itself connaturally complete, God too remains without turning God, being Father of his own radiance, not taking it on from outside, but having begotten it complete from the essence. 11.ν [Chapter title:] About those prattling that 'from the naming Father the essence of the Son himself is altered'. 11.1 Circling round the same things about the same things and to the utmost counterfeiting the beauty of the truth, without love of God they assert this too: 11.2 of which the names are different, of these the essences too must have been altered. 11.3 For he says: 'the word Father does not signify the [word] Son, nor again does the naming Son show the hypostasis of the Father'. 11.4 But let them hear, one thing, that, if the divine hypostases had not been made manifest by a corresponding designation, using what kind of sign would someone, not saying the designation of Father, have indicated both the Father himself and that he has a Son? pass_b_english: And indeed the whole sense of these words leans toward his becoming man. For when he said, “I am the Son of God,” and they retorted, “You blaspheme” (John 10:36), the Father ratified it for him: “This alone is my true Son.” That is what “this,” and “beloved,” and his being named “Son” with the article make plain. “In this one,” he says, “I was well pleased that through his becoming man salvation should be won for you.”

And even if someone takes “I was well pleased” of his Godhead, their sophism is made void. For not every expression spoken by God, and least of all about God the Word, yields a meaning by the custom of this world. Then again, if he said “in whom I was well pleased” of the Son who already existed, the good pleasure is not found to be the cause of his existence.

To make plainer what such an expression signifies, let us take as our witness the one who sings in Psalm 149, “For the Lord takes pleasure in his people” (Psalm 149:4). The good pleasure did not come about before the people, but after them. For he took pleasure in them, and sent them peace and grace, at the times when they served him rightly. When they did not, the reverse, as he now prophesies: “When he slew them, then they sought him” (Psalm 78:34). And in Psalm 44: “Their arm did not save them, but your right hand, and your arm, and the light of your face, because you took pleasure in them” (Psalm 44:3). Here he names the Son “the right hand and arm of God” and “the light of his face.” And in Psalm 106: “Remember us, Lord, in the good pleasure of your people” (Psalm 106:4).
On their saying, “If the unbegotten God is wholly generative, he did not beget from his essence,” and, “If his essence was changed into an offspring, the essence of God is not unchangeable.”

This too is theirs, a random and faulty argument, set down in words like these: “If the unbegotten God is wholly generative, the one begotten was not begotten from his essence, since his whole essence has the property of begetting, but not of being begotten.”

But let them hear this: “If the light is wholly generative, it does not beget its radiance from its essence but takes it on from outside, since its whole essence has the property of begetting, but not of being begotten.” But if the light does not take on its radiance from outside, but begets it from its whole essence without any interval, then neither did God acquire the Son from outside. He begot him from his whole hypostasis without any interval, since he is without body. That is why he is truly Father.

Again they press on, everywhere pursuing a course contrary to Scripture: “If the essence of God, by being transformed, is called offspring, then his essence is not unchangeable, since it was the change that brought about the Son’s own distinct being.”

But no one grants them leave to say even this. For the Scripture we have mentioned proves such talk foreign to Christians, and it stands against every heretical and most grievous disorder. For if light, by being transformed, becomes radiance, then light is not unchangeable, since the change brings about the radiance’s own distinct being. But if light has begotten radiance without being changed, remaining light itself and having from itself its radiance, complete and grown together with it, then God too remains God without turning, being Father of his own radiance. He did not take it on from outside, but begot it complete from his essence.
On those who prattle that, on the ground of the name “Father,” the essence of the Son himself is different.

Going round and round the same things on the same subjects, and counterfeiting the beauty of the truth at every point, they say this too, without love for God: things whose names differ must also differ in essence. For he says, “The word ‘Father’ does not signify the word ‘Son,’ nor does the name ‘Son’ show the hypostasis of the Father.”

But let them hear, first, this. If the divine hypostases had not been made known by fitting names, what sign could anyone have used to make known the Father himself, and that he has a Son, without saying the name “Father”? Or how, without naming the names “Son” and “Spirit,” could anyone have addressed the Son himself or the Spirit, and shown that the Son has a Father and that the Spirit is the Spirit of God?

And second, this. In the holy Trinity, apart from the one who truly is Father being called Father, and the one who was begotten by nature being called Only-begotten, and the one who is exactly what it has been called, and belongs to the Father, being named Spirit of God, all the other names stand the same: such as God, Lord, holy, righteous, good, light, life. lemmas.gloss: appropriation, making a thing one's own

choices.issue: Old draft broken, garbled and mis-referenced
choices.choice: Retranslated the whole section from the Greek. The old English cut 10.4 off with '[text ends abruptly]' and began a new paragraph mid-thought, though the Greek is whole; made νένευκε 'has been fully explained' (it leans toward); μετ' αὐτόν 'with them' (after them); κοσμικοῦ ἔθους 'cosmic custom'; τὸ εἰκαῖον καὶ πλημμελές 'appropriate and full of errors' (random and faulty); garbled 10.6 ('Scripture, having mentioned these things as belonging to others, opposes every heretic with great difficulty') and 11.4; and turned Didymus' second answer (Ἕτερον δέ, 11.5) into 'Another [thing they say]'. Wrong psalms: 'Psalm 140' for LXX 149 (English 149), 'Psalm 84' for LXX 43 (English 44), 'Psalm 103' for LXX 105 (English 106). Added Psalm 149:4, Psalm 44:3, Psalm 106:4 and John 10:36; kept Psalm 78:34.

choices.why: Greek Psalm numbers 149, 43, 105 converted to English numbers and checked by verse text.

choices.term: «οὗτος μόνος ἐστὶν ὁ υἱός μου γνήσιος»
choices.why: Didymus' paraphrase of the Father's voice, not a Bible verse; left in quotation marks as in the copy-text but given no reference.

choices.english: the reverse, as he now prophesies
choices.why: ἤ read as ᾗ ('as'), the only reading that lets the psalm quotation illustrate the reverse of good pleasure; see problems.

choices.english: from his essence / from its essence
choices.why: The Arian claim is that the Son is not begotten out of the Father's essence; 'essentially' would suggest 'basically' in English.

choices.english: the property of begetting, but not of being begotten
choices.why: Articular infinitives with ἔχω; 'property of' is English shape for 'has the begetting'.

ἰδιοποίησις, appropriation or making something one's own: the Arian says the change of essence would make the Son a thing of his own. Rendered so the sentence reads aloud; the same phrase for the radiance in 10.7.
The '6' is a printed line number in the copy-text (page debris); skipped.

choices.term: ἡ πατὴρ λέξις οὐ σημαίνει τὴν υἱός
choices.english: The word ‘Father’ does not signify the word ‘Son’
choices.why: The feminine article τήν agrees with an understood λέξιν; English repeats 'the word'. The stray mark ʹ at the end of the quotation in the copy-text is read as its closing quote.

choices.term: Ἀκουέτωσαν δέ, ἓν μέν … Ἕτερον δέ
choices.english: But let them hear, first, this … And second, this.
choices.why: Didymus' two-part answer; the old draft gave the second part to the opponents.
Dotted letter is an uncertain reading in the copy-text; the word is clear and translated.
The section ends mid-sentence; only the words it holds are translated, ending with an ellipsis.
